primer.text: You already know from everyday life that ice melts, puddles dry out and steam fogs a cold window. This topic turns that familiar experience into a precise particle picture: what solids, liquids and gases really are, and what exactly happens when a substance changes from one state to another. By the end you will be able to name every state change and explain it through the behaviour of particles.

modules.title: States of matter
modules.opening: Everything around you exists as a solid, a liquid or a gas, and the same substance can usually move between all three. Chemists explain the differences with a particle model, picturing every particle as a small solid sphere. How those spheres are arranged, how freely they move and how much energy they hold decide which state a material takes.
keyPoints: Solids, liquids and gases are the three states, and one substance can usually exist in each of them.
Melting and freezing happen at the melting point; boiling and condensing happen at the boiling point.
In the model, every particle is drawn as a small solid sphere, whatever the substance.
Solid particles sit in a regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions and very close together.
Liquid particles are randomly arranged but still close, moving around each other.
Gas particles are randomly arranged, far apart, and move quickly in all directions.

low.restatement: Solid particles sit in neat rows and only vibrate on the spot; liquid particles stay close but jostle past each other; gas particles fly far apart at speed.
low.analogy: Think of a full cinema: during the film everyone stays seated (solid), as they leave they shuffle past one another (liquid), and outside they scatter in every direction (gas).
low.examPointer: Learn the arrangement, movement and closeness rows for all three states; comparison questions ask for exactly those table entries.

medium.restatement: Arrangement runs from regular in solids to random in liquids and gases, while movement grows from vibration about fixed points to fast motion in all directions, carrying more energy as particles gain freedom and spacing widens.
medium.analogy: The cinema crowd still works: seated viewers only fidget, a departing queue shuffles sideways, and a scattered crowd crosses the foyer quickly, with energy rising at each stage.
medium.examPointer: State changes occur at the melting point and the boiling point, and individual atoms do not share the properties of the bulk material.

modules.title: Interconversion Between the States of Matter
sourceHeadings: Interconversion Between the States of Matter
modules.opening: Heat or cool a substance and it can switch between solid, liquid and gas, with a named change for each direction. Melting, boiling, evaporating, freezing, condensing and subliming all describe one underlying event: particles gaining or losing energy until their arrangement alters. Because no new substance forms at any point, every one of these changes is a physical change.
keyPoints: Changing state is a physical change: the particles stay the same and only the forces between them alter.
Stronger forces between particles need more energy to overcome, giving higher melting and boiling points.
Melting turns a solid to a liquid as absorbed heat becomes kinetic energy and particles vibrate more.
Boiling forms gas bubbles throughout the liquid at one temperature; evaporation happens at the surface across a range.
Freezing reverses melting at the same temperature, and sublimation turns a solid straight into a gas.

low.restatement: Adding heat melts a solid, then boils the liquid; removing heat condenses a gas, then freezes the liquid. A few solids skip the liquid stage and turn straight to gas.
low.analogy: An ice cube on a warm plate does it all: it melts into a puddle, the puddle dries to vapour, and cooling any stage sends it back the other way.
low.examPointer: Boiling happens at one fixed temperature while evaporation works at the surface across a range; that contrast is a favourite exam question.

medium.restatement: Each interconversion is named by its direction and achieved by energy transfer: heating supplies kinetic energy so particles break loose from fixed positions, while cooling lets particles lose energy and settle back into closer arrangements.
medium.analogy: Picture a car park at rush hour: heating empties the neat rows into freely moving traffic, and cooling funnels the traffic back into ordered spaces.
medium.examPointer: Questions may draw a state change with reversible arrows, so name each direction separately and state how the change is achieved.

glossary.definition: The fixed temperature at which a pure substance melts and freezes.
The fixed temperature at which a liquid boils, with gas bubbles forming throughout the liquid.
A simple representation in which all particles are drawn as small solid spheres.
Rapid back-and-forth movement of a particle about a fixed position, as in solids.
The change from liquid to gas at the surface, across a range of temperatures below the boiling point.
The change from gas to liquid on cooling, when particles lack the energy to bounce apart again.
The direct change from solid to gas, shown by only a few solids such as iodine.
A change in which the particles stay the same and only the forces between them alter.
